869.title: The thirty at the Harmandir
869.hook: tradition says thirty Sikhs with Baba Gurbakhsh Singh stayed to defend the Harmandir
869.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Baba Gurbakhsh Singh and his companions among the martyrs, and at the Harmandir Sahib complex a place near the Akal Takht bears his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dal Khalsa took Sirhind, the city of the Sahibzade's deaths. Your line was the tide turned. Today, the turn isn't finished yet.

Word reaches Amritsar that the invader is coming back. The main bands of the Khalsa are far off. The Harmandir still bears the scars of the last time. Anyone with sense would pack up and go, and people do go, down the roads out of the city. But tradition says a small group stays, around an older Sikh named Baba Gurbakhsh Singh. Not an army. A handful. Tradition gives the number as thirty.
screen: `THE INVADER RETURNS.` → `THE BANDS ARE FAR AWAY.` → `A HANDFUL STAYS.`

segments.voice: Start with what they were not doing. They were not expecting to win. Nobody in this story imagines thirty people stopping an army. That's what makes it worth telling. Then, what they were doing: keeping a place from being left empty. The Harmandir was where the Guru's word was sung, day after day. Tradition says that before the army arrived, the thirty prepared the way Sikhs prepare for anything serious: they bathed, they prayed, they listened to the Guru's word. When the army came, they went out to meet it rather than wait behind the walls. And they died, every one, tradition says, with Baba Gurbakhsh Singh. Then, how Sikhs keep it. Near the Akal Takht in Amritsar there's a place that bears his name, a shaheedi bunga, a martyrs' tower, remembering him and the others. People praying at the Harmandir today walk past the spot that remembers the thirty. And last, the part for an ordinary day. Not everyone is asked to be brave in a big way. Plenty of duties are small and unwatched: the one who stays to lock up, the one who keeps showing up when everyone else drifts off, the one who stays on the phone. The thirty are remembered for staying where they were needed when there was no hope of a reward. Thirty stood.

Picture yourself staying with it today, even when drifting off would be easy, and feel your feet on the floor while you hold it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

870.title: Lahore, 1765
870.hook: Sikh chiefs entered Lahore and struck coins in the Gurus' names
870.howItsDone: Coins struck by Sikh rulers in the Gurus' names are kept in museums and collections, and Sikhs still use the phrase deg teg fateh for the ideals of feeding and protecting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shaheedi bunga, remembering those who stayed when staying meant dying. Your line was thirty stood. Today, a city and a coin.

Check the coins in a pocket or a purse. Whose face is on them? Whose name? A coin goes where no army goes: into markets, kitchens and strangers' hands. So when Sikh chiefs rode into Lahore, the great city where Sikhs had been hunted, tortured and killed, there was an obvious next step, the thing anyone holding a city does. Strike a coin. The question is whose name to put on it.
screen: `A COIN TRAVELS FARTHER THAN AN ARMY.` → `SIKH CHIEFS RIDE INTO LAHORE.` → `WHOSE NAME GOES ON THE COIN?`

segments.voice: First, the city. Lahore was the seat of governors this path has met in the hard years, with its prisons and its executions. Now Sikh chiefs held it. Second, the coin. Tradition says the coins they struck carried no chief's name. Instead they carried a short verse in Persian, the language of coins and courts, naming Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. In the common telling, the verse says that the deg, the teg and the fateh, along with the help that came without delay, were received from Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. Third, the three words, which are worth slowing down for. Deg is a big cooking pot, the kind used in the langar, the free kitchen. Teg is a sword. Fateh is victory. So the pot comes before the sword. Feeding people is named first, defending them second, and the victory is credited to the Gurus. A chief could have stamped his own name and claimed the win. This coin says it wasn't theirs to claim. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Whatever people put their name on tells others what they think they own. Sikhs remember this coin as one that pointed past the people who made it. The gurus' coin.

871.title: Delhi, 1783
871.hook: Baghel Singh camped at Delhi and marked the sites where gurdwaras like Sis Ganj now stand
871.howItsDone: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, is visited by Sikhs and others; Baghel Singh's role in marking Delhi's Sikh sites is told in Sikh histories.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lahore, and coins struck in the Gurus' names: deg, teg, fateh. Your line was the gurus' coin. Today, the Khalsa reaches the capital.

A Sikh army is camped outside Delhi, the seat of the Mughal emperors. The court is nervous. The army's leader, Baghel Singh, could ask for a great deal: money, land, a share of the city's wealth. The court wants him gone. Tradition says that along with a share of the city's taxes, he asked for something stranger: to stay a while, and to find and mark the places in the city where the Gurus had been.
screen: `A SIKH ARMY OUTSIDE DELHI.` → `THE COURT WANTS HIM GONE.` → `HE ASKS FOR THE GURUS' PLACES.`

segments.voice: Why Delhi? Guru Tegh Bahadur was put to death there, in the middle of the city; Sikhs remember it as the price of standing up for other people's freedom to worship. Sikhs knew roughly where. But the city had moved on, and shops, houses and other buildings stood on ground Sikhs remembered as sacred. Tradition says Baghel Singh set about finding the exact spots: where the Guru was beheaded, where his body was secretly cremated, where other Gurus had stayed. Some of it, tradition says, came down to asking people who remembered. Then the places were marked, so that gurdwaras could rise there. The name you can still find on a map of Delhi is Sis Ganj. Sis is an old word for head, still used in Punjabi. Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib stands in Chandni Chowk, a crowded old market street, on the place Sikhs remember as where the Guru gave his head. There's a deeper day on this path later for the Guru's death itself; today's story is the marking. Armies come and go, and their camps are forgotten. The gurdwaras he marked still draw people in. He used his one moment of power to make sure a memory had a place to live. Marking the places.

872.title: Ala Singh and Patiala
872.hook: the Phulkian chiefs founded the states of Patiala, Nabha and Jind
872.howItsDone: The history of the Phulkian states of Patiala, Nabha and Jind, and the tradition of Guru Har Rai's blessing of Phul, is told in Sikh and Punjabi histories.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Delhi, where Baghel Singh marked the places the Gurus had been. Your line was marking the places. Today, a different kind of founding.

A mud fort goes up on open ground in the Malwa country, south of the Sutlej. A well. A few houses around it. A market that starts with a handful of stalls. That's how some towns start, and Patiala, now a busy city in Indian Punjab, is remembered as starting something like that, around a fort built by a Sikh chief named Ala Singh. His family line had a name of its own, and a story that goes back to a Guru.
screen: `A FORT ON OPEN GROUND.` → `A WELL, A FEW HOUSES, A MARKET.` → `THE TOWN THAT BECAME PATIALA.`

segments.voice: The family were the Phulkians, named for an ancestor called Phul. Phul means flower. Tradition tells a story about him as a small boy. He was brought, with his brother, before Guru Har Rai. The boys were hungry, and Phul patted his stomach. Tradition says the Guru took it as a sign and blessed him: his descendants would have enough, and would feed many. The Phulkian families remember that blessing as the root of what came after. And what came after: Ala Singh, one of Phul's line, built up his holdings in these hard decades and founded the town and state of Patiala. Other branches of the same family founded the states of Nabha and Jind. So in the middle of the decades of persecution, some Sikh families weren't only riding and hiding. They were laying out streets, digging wells, building forts and markets. Then, honesty. Ala Singh's story isn't a simple hero's tale. He dealt with more than one power to keep his state alive, and tradition records that this put him at odds at times with other Sikh leaders. This path tells it with that tension left in. Last, the small piece. Every town you've lived in began somewhere: a crossing, a fort, a mill, a well. Someone chose that spot, and people kept coming. Towns begin.

873.title: Mothers in Mannu's prison
873.hook: the Ardas remembers Sikh women imprisoned with their children who kept faith
873.howItsDone: Sikh women who kept their faith are remembered when the Ardas is said, standing, at the end of services and at many daily and family occasions; a site in Lahore also keeps their memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a fort, a well, and the town of Patiala beginning. Your line was towns begin. Today, a harder story, told gently.

In gurdwaras, a congregation stands, and someone leads the Ardas, the prayer that remembers the community's history out loud. Part of it calls to mind people who suffered and kept their faith. Among them are women, the Singhnian. Not named one by one. Remembered together. Tradition places them in a prison in Lahore, under a governor named Mir Mannu, with their children beside them. This is a heavy story, and it's told here carefully.
screen: `THE ARDAS, SAID STANDING.` → `IT REMEMBERS SIKH WOMEN, TOGETHER.` → `A PRISON IN LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Here is what tradition says happened. In the hard years, the governor at Lahore, Mir Mannu, had Sikh women seized from villages and held in prison with their small children. They were set to grind grain on heavy hand mills, with little to eat. And they were told there was a way out: give up the Sikh faith. Tradition says they refused. Then, how they endured. Tradition says that while they ground the grain, they recited the Guru's hymns, the words keeping time with the stone. Whatever else was taken, the words stayed with them. Then the worst part, which Sikh memory doesn't hide. Tradition says their children were killed in front of them, and still they did not give up their faith. The Ardas remembers Singhnian, Sikh women, beside the men who gave their lives and did not give up their faith, and some who lead it add words for the mothers whose children were killed before them. It isn't said for shock. It's said so that no one forgets what was carried. And where they're remembered now. In Lahore, a place called the Shaheed Ganj of the Singhnian marks the memory. When the Ardas is said, in a village gurdwara or a great one, these women are in the room. Their story is kept not as a tale of what was done to them, but of what they held on to. The mothers kept faith.

segments.voice: Bring to mind any mother, anywhere, carrying more than she should have to: in a war, in a hospital corridor, in a prison visiting room, at a kitchen table with a pile of bills. You don't need to know her; just hold her in mind, with her children. If you pray, pray for her in your own way, or say Waheguru on each breath out; if you don't, simply hold her there.

874.title: The more he cut
874.hook: a Sikh saying of those days: the persecutor was a sickle, the Sikhs a crop that grew back
874.howItsDone: The saying about Mannu's sickle is still repeated in Sikh history talks and Punjabi retellings of the eighteenth century as a picture of the community's resilience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mothers in Mannu's prison, remembered in the Ardas. Your line was the mothers kept faith. Today, what people said about that same governor.

Mow a lawn on Saturday, and by the next weekend it's back. Cut a pot of mint down to stubs, and it pushes out new leaves. Gardeners know this about some plants: cutting doesn't finish them. Now carry that into Punjab in the hard years, when the governor at Lahore was hunting Sikhs. Out of those years comes a short saying, passed from mouth to mouth, that turns the whole terrible situation into a picture from the fields.
screen: `MOW IT, AND IT COMES BACK.` → `THE HARD YEARS UNDER MANNU.` → `A SAYING FROM THE FIELDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the saying in plain English, since it's a Punjabi folk verse and loses its rhyme in translation. Mannu is our sickle. We are the crop he cuts. And the more Mannu cuts us, the more we grow. Take it in pieces. First, the sickle: a curved, handheld farm tool, used at harvest by people who have cut wheat all their lives. The saying takes a feared governor and turns him into a tool in a field. Not a dragon. Not a demon. A sickle. That alone is a kind of courage, and a kind of humor, the dark humor people find when things are at their worst. Second, the crop. The Sikhs picture themselves as something growing, rooted in the soil of Punjab, not as soldiers or victims. A crop belongs to the land. Third, the turn. The more he cuts, the more we grow: the gardener's knowledge from the hook, said in defiance. Cutting doesn't finish what has roots. Sikh tradition says the community did keep coming back through those years; that's the story this path has been following, from the hiding to Sirhind. Fourth, the plant itself. The Punjabi word in the saying, soe, is often glossed as dill, a kitchen-garden herb, not a field of wheat. Some readers hear it simply as a crop. Either way, the picture is of something small and green that comes back when it's cut, like the mint in the hook. We grow back.

segments.voice: Think of something that cut you back recently, a no, a loss, a plan that fell apart, and picture it as a sickle, just a tool that passed through. 875.title: How we know this
875.hook: the stories of this century come down through later Sikh chroniclers, Persian records and family memory
875.howItsDone: Historians of the Sikh eighteenth century read Sikh chronicles, Persian court histories and oral tradition side by side; in gurdwaras, the same history is carried by the Ardas and by talks called katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mannu as a sickle and the Sikhs as a crop. Your line was we grow back. Today, a step back from the stories, to ask where they come from.

Listen back over the last few weeks on this path and count how often you heard two words: tradition says. Tradition says a brick struck the invader. Tradition says thirty stood. Tradition says the mothers recited the hymns while they ground the grain. Those two words have been doing quiet work all along. They signal that a story has come down by a particular road. So today, a different kind of lesson: not what happened, but how we know this.
screen: `TWO WORDS: TRADITION SAYS.` → `A STORY COMES DOWN BY A ROAD.` → `NOT WHAT HAPPENED, BUT HOW WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: There are three main roads. The first is the Sikh chroniclers. Long tellings of this century were written down by Sikhs, some well after the events, from what their families and elders had told them. They wrote as insiders, with love and grief, and kept names and places other records leave out. Tomorrow you'll meet one of them. The second road is the Persian records. The courts and governors of the time kept histories in Persian, and so did some writers who traveled with the invading armies. They wrote from the other side, some with contempt, calling the Sikhs rebels. But they sometimes confirm that a battle happened or a city fell, even while telling it their own way. The third road is memory. Families who passed stories down. Places like the bunga by the Akal Takht and the gurdwaras of Delhi, which hold a story in stone. And the Ardas, which carries the martyrs into the congregations that say it. Each road has its strengths and blind spots. Insiders remember what mattered to them; outsiders record what mattered to theirs. Memory keeps the heart of a story and sometimes rounds off its numbers. So when historians set the roads side by side, they find places where all three agree, and places where they don't. That's why this path says tradition says. It isn't a sneer, and it isn't a verdict. It's an honest label for how a story arrived. How do we know.
screen: `SIKH CHRONICLERS, WRITING LATER.` · `PERSIAN RECORDS FROM THE OTHER SIDE.` · `MEMORY: FAMILIES, PLACES, THE ARDAS.` · `SETTING THE ROADS SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `HOW DO WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone older who carries a story you only half know, a grandparent, an old neighbor, someone at your gurdwara, church or mosque, and wonder what they saw that you didn't. Shape one simple question you'd like to ask them, what was it like when, who was there when, and hold the question and their face for the rest of the sit. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
itihas, history. Sikh chroniclers, Persian records, and memory kept in families, places and the Ardas: the three roads this story of the past has come down to us by. Today's word.
Your line: how do we know. Asking where a story came from is a way of taking it seriously. See you tomorrow.
